raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="2" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|VECTOR ANALYSIS|963|}}</noinclude> rigid body about a fixed point <math>\text{O}</math>. As explained under {{sc|Mechanics}}, the state of motion at any instant is specified by a vector <math>\overrightarrow{\text{OI}}</math> representing the angular velocity. The instantaneous velocity of any other point <math>\text{P}</math> of the body is completely determined by the two vectors <math>\overrightarrow{\text{OI}}</math> and <math>\overrightarrow{\text{OP}}</math>, viz. it is a vector normal to the plane of <math>\text{OI}</math> and <math>\text{OP}</math>, whose absolute magnitude is <math>\text{OI}\,.\,\text{OP}\,.\sin\theta</math>, where <math>\theta</math> denotes the inclination of <math>\text{OP}</math> to <math>\text{OI}</math>, and its sense is that due to a right-handed rotation about <math>\text{OI}</math>. A vector derived according to this rule from any two given vectors <math>\mathbf{A}</math>, <math>\mathbf{B}</math> is called their ''vector product'', and is denoted by <math>\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}</math> or by <math>[\mathbf{AB}]</math>. This type of combination is frequent in electro-magnetism; thus if <math>\mathbf{C}</math> be the current and <math>\mathbf{B}</math> the magnetic induction, at any point of a conductor, the mechanical force on the latter is represented by the vector <math>[\mathbf{CB}]</math>. It will be noticed in the above kinematical example that if the rôles of the two vectors <math>\text{OI}</math>, <math>\text{OP}</math> were interchanged, the resulting vector would have the same absolute magnitude as before, but its sense would be reversed. Hence
{{block center|<math>[\mathbf{AB}]=-[\mathbf{BA}],</math> . . . . . (6)}}
so that the commutative law does ''not'' hold with respect to vector products. On the other hand, the distributive law applies, for we have
{{block center|<math>[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})]=[\mathbf{AB}]+[\mathbf{AC}],</math> . . . . . (7)}}
as may be proved without difficulty by considering the kinematical interpretation.

[[File:eb1911 v27 p0991 c1f1.png|center|288px]]

Various types of triple products may also present themselves, the most important being the scalar product of two vectors, one of which is itself given as a vector product. Thus <math>\mathbf{A}[\mathbf{BC}]</math> is equal in absolute value to the volume of the parallelepiped constructed on three edges <math>\text{OA}</math>, <math>\text{OB}</math>, <math>\text{OC}</math> drawn from a point <math>\text{O}</math> to represent the vectors <math>\mathbf{A}</math>, <math>\mathbf{B}</math>, <math>\mathbf{C}</math> respectively, and it is positive or negative according as the lines <math>\text{OA}</math>, <math>\text{OB}</math>, <math>\text{OC}</math> follow one another in right- or left-handed cyclical order. It follows that
{{block center|<math>\mathbf{A}[\mathbf{BC}]=\mathbf{B}[\mathbf{CA}]=-\mathbf{B}[\mathbf{AC}]=\text{\&c.}</math> . . . (8)}}

In order to exhibit the correspondence between the shorthand methods of vector analysis and the more familiar formulae of Cartesian geometry, we take a right-handed system of three mutually perpendicular axes <math>\text{O}x</math>, <math>\text{O}y</math>, <math>\text{O}z</math>, and adopt three fundamental ''unit-vectors'' <math>i, j, k</math>, having the positive directions of these axes respectively. As regards the scalar products of these unit-vectors, we have, by (4),
{{block center|<math>i^2=j^2=k^2=1,\ jk=kj=ji=0.</math> . . . . (9)}}
Any other vector <math>\mathbf{A}</math> is expressed in terms of its scalar projections <math>\text{A}_1</math>, <math>\text{A}_2</math>, <math>\text{A}_3</math> on the co-ordinate axes by the formula
{{block center|<math>\mathbf{A}=i\text{A}_1+j\text{A}_2+k\text{A}_3.</math> . . . . . . (10)}}
For the scalar product of any two vectors we have
{{block center|<math>\mathbf{AB}=(i\text{A}_1+j\text{A}_2+k\text{A}_3)(i\text{B}_1+j\text{B}_2+k\text{B}_3)=\text{A}_1\text{B}_1+\text{A}_2\text{B}_2+\text{A}_3\text{B}_3,</math>(11)}}
as appears on developing the product and making use of (9). In particular, forming the scalar square of <math>\mathbf{A}</math> we have
{{block center|<math>A^2=\text{A}_1{}^2+\text{A}_2{}^2+\text{A}_3{}^2,</math> . . . . . (12)}}
where <math>A</math> denotes the absolute value of <math>\mathbf{A}</math>.

Again, the rule for vector products, applied to the fundamental units, gives
{{block center|<math>\left.\begin{array}{c}[i^2]=[j^2]=[k^2]=0,\\ [jk]=-[kj]=i,\ [ki]=-[ik]=j,\ [ij]=-[ji]=k.\end{array}\right\}</math> (13)}}
Hence
{{block center|<math>[\mathbf{AB}]=[(i\text{A}_1+j\text{A}_2+k\text{A}_3)(i\text{B}_1+j\text{B}_2+k\text{B}_3)]</math>}}
{{block center|<math>=i(\text{A}_2\text{B}_3-\text{A}_3\text{B}_2)+j(\text{A}_3\text{B}_1-\text{A}_1\text{B}_3)+k(\text{A}_1\text{B}_2-\text{A}_2\text{B}_1)</math>}}
{{block center|<math>=-[\mathbf{BA}].</math> . . . . . . . . . . . . (14)}}
The correspondence with the formulae which occur in the analytical theory of rotations, &c., will be manifest. If we form the scalar product of a third vector <math>\mathbf{C}</math> into <math>[\mathbf{AB}]</math>, we obtain
{{block center|<math>\mathbf{C}[\mathbf{AB}]=\begin{vmatrix}\text{A}_1, & \text{B}_1, & \text{C}_1\\ \text{A}_2, & \text{B}_2, & \text{C}_2\\ \text{A}_3, & \text{B}_3, & \text{C}_3\end{vmatrix}</math> . . . . . . (15)}}
in agreement with the geometrical interpretation already given.

In such subjects as hydrodynamics and electricity we are introduced to the notion of scalar and vector ''fields''. With every point <math>\text{P}</math> of the region under consideration there are associated certain scalars (''e.g.'' density, electric or magnetic potential) and vectors (''e.g.'' fluid velocity, electric or magnetic force) which are regarded as functions of the position of <math>\text{P}</math>. If we treat the partial-differential operators <math>\partial/\partial x</math>, <math>\partial/\partial y</math>, <math>\partial/\partial z</math>, where <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, <math>z</math> are the co-ordinates of <math>\text{P}</math>, as if they were scalar quantities, we are led to some remarkable and significant expressions. Thus if we write
{{block center|<math>\nabla=\left(i\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+j\frac{\partial}{\partial y}+k\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\right),</math> . . . . (16)}}
and operate on a scalar function <math>\phi</math>, we obtain the vector
{{block center|<math>\nabla\phi=i\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}+j\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}+k\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}.</math> . . . . . (17)}}
This is called the ''gradient'' of <math>\phi</math> and sometimes denoted by “grad <math>\phi</math>”; its direction is that in which <math>\phi</math> most rapidly increases, and its magnitude is equal to the corresponding rate of increase. Thus
{{block center|<math>(\nabla\phi)^2=\left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}\right)^2.</math> . . . . (18)}}
A repetition of the operation <math>\nabla</math> gives
{{block center|<math>\nabla^2\phi=\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial y^2}+\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial z^2}.</math> . . . . . (19)}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
